::: {.lead-note}

Most of what makes an empirical paper credible never appears in its abstract. It
sits in how a variable was built, which units were kept, and what the author did
when the data refused to line up with the question. These notes are about that
layer. Each one takes a single paper, or a single problem I have run into
myself, and asks what the measurement problem was, what was done about it, what
the fix cost, and whether it can be reused on Indonesian data.

They are notes rather than reviews. The point is not to judge the paper but to
extract the technique.

:::

::: {.note}

The notes below are in preparation. Each will be published here as it is
finished.

:::

## In preparation

::: {.insight-item}

### Village Boundaries Do Not Hold Still: PODES as a Panel
Two decades of *pemekaran* mean that a village observed in 2005 and a village
carrying the same code in 2024 are frequently not the same place. What that does
to a village panel, how far a constant-boundary crosswalk repairs it, and how
much of the sample does not survive the repair.

:::

::: {.insight-item}

### Two Crosswalks for the Same Problem
Cassidy (2025) published a village merge crosswalk covering PODES 1993 to 2021.
I built one independently, anchored on 2005 boundaries, for a different purpose.
Where the two approaches agree, where they diverge, and what the divergence
implies for anyone choosing between them.

:::

::: {.insight-item}

### From an Intensity Surface to a Village-Level Shock
Seismic intensity arrives as a raster, and treatment has to be defined on
administrative units. The choices made in between, aggregation rule, threshold,
and timing against the survey window, are measurement decisions with real
consequences for the estimate, not technical housekeeping.

:::
